Stateless random numbers

Source: vignettes/zurand.Rmd
zurand.Rmd
library(zurand)

One idea

R’s generators are stateful. set.seed() fixes a starting point, and every call to runif() or rnorm() moves a hidden cursor, .Random.seed. What you get depends on everything drawn before: add one rnorm() call early in a script and every later number changes; split a loop across workers and the numbers depend on how the work was divided.

zurand has no cursor. A value is a pure function of a key and the draw’s position:

key <- rng_key(2026L)
rng_uniform(key, 3L)
#> [1] 0.15037421 0.91830293 0.06342998
rng_uniform(key, 3L)          # same key, same values
#> [1] 0.15037421 0.91830293 0.06342998
rng_uniform(key, 6L)[1:3]     # draw i does not depend on how many you ask for
#> [1] 0.15037421 0.91830293 0.06342998

Nothing is consumed, so nothing has to be passed along, saved or restored.

Many streams: key vectors and folding

Independent streams come from independent keys. Ask for a vector of them, and a sampler returns one column per key:

keys <- rng_key(2026L, n = 3L)
rng_normal(keys, 4L)
#>              [,1]       [,2]        [,3]
#> [1,]  0.006686381 -2.2711494  0.42616283
#> [2,] -1.233412249 -0.2468333  0.05688975
#> [3,]  0.591067060  0.9256739 -1.02992948
#> [4,]  0.835300390  1.1623784  0.68884687

Or derive a key from what a piece of work is, with rng_fold(). The same data always derives the same key, so a computation can name its parts instead of counting them:

chain_key <- function(chain) rng_fold(key, paste("chain", chain))
rng_normal(chain_key(3), 2L)
#> [1] -1.8032411  0.0360179
rng_normal(chain_key(3), 2L)  # chain 3 gets the same numbers every run
#> [1] -1.8032411  0.0360179

Folding is typed: rng_fold(key, 1) and rng_fold(key, "1") differ, while 1L and 1 agree.

Reproducible no matter how the work is split

Because every task’s numbers come from its own key, the result cannot depend on scheduling. Here is a small bootstrap, one key per replicate. It gives the same answer serially, in any order, or spread over workers:

x <- c(2.1, 3.4, 1.9, 5.6, 4.2, 3.3, 2.8, 4.9)
boot_mean <- function(b) {
  i <- rng_integer(rng_fold(key, b), length(x), 1L, length(x))
  mean(x[i])
}
serial <- vapply(1:200, boot_mean, numeric(1))

# The same replicates computed in a random order, then put back in place.
order <- sample(200)
shuffled <- numeric(200)
shuffled[order] <- vapply(order, boot_mean, numeric(1))
identical(serial, shuffled)
#> [1] TRUE

With parallel::mclapply() or future.apply::future_lapply() in place of vapply() the values are the same again: no worker needs a seed, and none can disturb another. zurand’s own threaded fills work the same way: rng_threads() changes the speed, never the values.

Engines

A key records its engine:

engine what it is
"xoshiro256pp" (default) xoshiro256++, reseeded from Philox every 512 values; the fastest
"philox4x64" Philox4x64-10, counter-based: each value computed from its position
"threefry4x64" Threefry4x64-13, counter-based

All three give the same guarantees. Changing engine changes every value, so name it when a stream has to outlive a change of default:

k <- rng_key(2026L, engine = "philox4x64")
attr(k, "engine")
#> [1] "philox4x64"

Bit-identical everywhere

The same key gives the same bits on Linux (glibc and musl), macOS and Windows, on x86_64 and ARM, at any thread count and with or without SIMD. That is enforced, not assumed. zurand computes the exp() and log1p() its normal sampler needs with its own port of fdlibm instead of the platform’s library, which rounds differently from system to system, and it keeps compilers from fusing multiply-adds, which would change results by a rounding step. Every CI platform checks known answers and hashes of whole streams.

Each key also carries a stream version:

attr(key, "stream")
#> [1] 1

The output of every (engine, stream) pair is frozen. If a stream ever needed correcting, the fix would ship as a new version for new keys, and existing keys, including saved ones, would go on producing exactly what they always have.

Interop

rng_key_from_r() is the one function that reads R’s own generator. Use it to turn a set.seed() into a key:

set.seed(1)
rng_key_from_r()
#> <rng_key> rng_key[5f43830b43f86031e8804e4492a6849d]

Packages can use the same streams from C or C++, from their own threads, through the API in zurand.h; see the README.
